author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: A particle-accelerator accident drops eight people into a succession of private worlds, each ruled by one bystander's inner reality — a bigot's, a paranoid's, a puritan's — forcing the question of which reality is true.
page_summary:
When a Bevatron beam malfunctions, eight visitors fall through a shared delusion. They pass through one subjective universe after another, each structured by the consciousness of a member of the group: a devout believer's world where prayer works and God literally watches from the sky, a prude's world where whole categories of things have been abolished, a paranoid's world where every object plots against them. The physics of each realm follows its ruler's convictions.

This is PKD's clearest early statement of the multiple-realities problem — the idea that consciousness structures the world, and that no one projection is privileged over another. What we call objective reality, the novel implies, is only the statistical averaging of countless minds pressing on the world at once. The horror is that there may be no ground truth to return to.

Published in 1957, it is among the earliest novels PKD later ranked with his strongest, and the template for the reality-instability that would drive Time Out of Joint, Ubik, and much of the work to come.

biography_events.event: Publishes Eye in the Sky, one of the early SF novels he later grouped among his strongest pre-1962 books; the novel's sky imagery anticipates his later third-eye and sun-of-righteousness language.
In 1979, PKD wrote 4 letters to Sherie Rush, turning the correspondence into a sustained discussion of the science-fiction community and religion and theology.
